title: Freshwater turtle

names.note: Dictionary: 'freshwater turtle'. A general word; the dictionary does not split it by species.

scientificName: Chelidae: Emydura, Myuchelys, Elseya and Chelodina species

identification.basis: The dictionary defines ngujay simply as 'freshwater turtle' and keeps ngawiya for the sea turtle. It is most likely a general word for all the river turtles. On the upper Mitchell those are chiefly the northern yellow-faced turtle (Emydura tanybaraga) and the saw-shelled turtle (Myuchelys latisternum), with snapping turtles (Elseya) and the northern snake-necked turtle (Chelodina rugosa) also recorded. Whether speakers had separate words for these is not recorded.

summary: **[Ngujay](word:ngujay)** is the Kuku Yalanji word for the freshwater turtle [ref:hershberger1982], the river turtle of the creeks and waterholes, as opposed to *[ngawiya](word:ngawiya)*, the [sea turtle](entry:sea-turtle). Bloomfield Kuku Yalanji went to the freshwater streams for '[eelfish](entry:eels) and freshwater tortoise', especially in the [dry season](entry:seasons) [ref:anderson1996]. They caught turtles on bark [lines](entry:hooks-and-lines) with [lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) thorn hooks, and by the 1970s by diving with goggles and a steel rod [ref:anderson1996]. Across North Queensland Roth found river turtles caught by hand or with small [nets](entry:nets); on the Palmer River they were killed by breaking the neck [ref:roth1901]. The upper Mitchell around [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) is turtle country, with northern yellow-faced and saw-shelled turtles the commonest kinds on record [ref:ala].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
The dictionary gives **[ngujay](word:ngujay)** 'freshwater turtle' [ref:hershberger1982]. It is a different animal and a different word from the [sea turtle](entry:sea-turtle), **[ngawiya](word:ngawiya)** [ref:hershberger1982]. The shell of a turtle is **[kadan](word:kadan)**. The more general word **[dumbul](word:dumbul)** covers 'any hard covering such as bark of a tree, crust of bread, shell of turtle' [ref:hershberger1982].

Older English writers called river turtles **'tortoises'**, and Roth and Anderson both use that word. When they write 'freshwater tortoise', they mean ngujay [ref:roth1901] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
The two river turtles you are most likely to meet on the upper Mitchell are these.

- **Northern yellow-faced turtle** (*Emydura tanybaraga*). A short-necked turtle with a shell up to about 28.5 cm. A light yellow band runs from the eye back to above the ear, and another from the corner of the mouth along the neck. The shell is light to dark brown with a yellow or white rim, and the belly plate is bone-coloured [ref:wp-emydura].
- **Saw-shelled turtle** (*Myuchelys latisternum*). The back edge of the shell stays **saw-toothed** all its life, and the neck is covered in **pointed bumps**. Females grow to 28 cm of shell, males to about 18 cm. It is mainly a meat-eater, taking fish, tadpoles, frogs and crustaceans, and it will even tear up and eat cane toads. It can give off a strong smell and **bites hard** when handled [ref:wp-sawshell].

sections.heading: Where it lives
sections.body:
River turtles live in the permanent pools, slow reaches, billabongs and [paperbark](entry:paperbark) swamps of the rivers [ref:wp-emydura]. The saw-shelled turtle ranges through rivers, streams, swamps and lagoons from Cape York to northern New South Wales [ref:wp-sawshell].

**Karma Waters and the upper Mitchell.** The Atlas of Living Australia has northern yellow-faced turtle records within 30 km of the [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) homestead, one of them about 11 km to the west, and a snapping turtle (*Elseya*) recorded about 25 km to the south-east. About 30 km east, on the Mitchell, a 1973 museum survey collected large series of both northern yellow-faced and saw-shelled turtles. A northern snake-necked turtle and a few Krefft's turtles have also been recorded in the upper Mitchell country [ref:ala]. Look for them in the long, permanent pools of the river.

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body:
At Bloomfield, freshwater tortoise was a **dry-season** food. Inland groups, which camped on sandy creek beds in the dry, split into small family groups and set up temporary 'branch' camps to go after [eelfish](entry:eels), tortoises, [wallabies](entry:wallaby) and [goannas](entry:goanna). Coastal people made seasonal trips inland to the freshwater streams 'for eelfish and freshwater tortoise' [ref:anderson1996].

Saw-shelled turtles nest from **September to December**, laying several clutches of 9–20 eggs that hatch in about 60 days [ref:wp-sawshell]. Roth recorded that across North Queensland turtle eggs were eaten 'whenever found' [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body: **Meat and eggs.** Ngujay was hunted for food: at Bloomfield it was one of the foods small family groups went after from their temporary dry-season camps [ref:anderson1996]. Its eggs (*[diburr](word:diburr)*, which also means 'seed') were eaten too [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901]. The dictionary's word *[minya](word:minya)* covers 'meat, eggs (protein food)' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: How it was caught and cooked
sections.body:
**By hand and with small [nets](entry:nets) (North Queensland generally).** Roth's summary is simple: 'Tortoises are caught in the hands or with small nets' [ref:roth1901]. His small folding hand-nets, described for fish, were worked by one person groping about the shallower waterholes with the net held in front or at the side [ref:roth1901].

**[Hook and line](entry:hooks-and-lines) (Bloomfield Kuku Yalanji)** [ref:anderson1996]:

1. Make a line from the bark of *Sterculia quadrifolia*.
2. Make a hook from a **[lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) thorn**.
3. Bait it with [grubs](entry:witchetty-grub), [small freshwater prawns](entry:cherabin) or small [frogs](entry:frogs).
4. Fish the freshwater creeks and waterholes. Lines were used here for turtle, [eelfish](entry:eels), [catfish](entry:catfish) and perch, and this was mostly women's work.

**Diving (Bloomfield Kuku Yalanji, late 1970s).** In the inland creeks people dived for freshwater eelfish and turtles, using **diving goggles and a flexible steel rod** [ref:anderson1996]. *[Mala-kural](word:mala-kural)* is 'a good diver' [ref:hershberger1982].

**Feeling with the feet.** Roth recorded people groping carefully along the mud with their feet to catch catfish on the Georgina River [ref:roth1901]. None of the sources describes feeling for turtles the same way on Kuku Yalanji country.

**Killing.** Two neighbouring methods are recorded [ref:roth1901]:

1. **Palmer River (Koko-minni):** pull the head well forwards, then **break the neck upwards and backwards**.
2. **Behind Princess Charlotte Bay:** push a stiff wooden bristle through the nostril into the brain and spinal cavity, and work it up and down.

**Cooking.** At Bloomfield, reptiles were cooked **straight on the fire** after the body had been bashed with an axe to break the bones [ref:anderson1996]. Roth describes the simplest cooking as laying the food 'on and in the hot ashes' [ref:roth1901], the dictionary's *[dindal](word:dindal)* 'to roast on coals'; *[nulu](word:nulu)* is 'ashes' and *[ngunjil](word:ngunjil)* 'hot coals or hot ashes' [ref:hershberger1982]. Bigger animals went into the [stone oven](entry:earth-oven) (*[kurrma](word:kurrma)*). Hot stones were lifted with lawyer-cane tongs into a pit, and the meat, with eucalyptus, acacia or wild-ginger leaves, was set in a bark trough on the stones. More hot stones went around and on top, then [tea-tree bark](entry:paperbark), and everything was covered with sand or earth for several hours [ref:anderson1996]. Food that is 'well cooked, done' is *[jani](word:jani)* [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
**Turtles bite.** The saw-shelled turtle bites hard when handled [ref:wp-sawshell]. Keep fingers away from the head.

**Crocodile water.** Diving and groping in waterholes is exactly what Crocwise warns against wherever [saltwater crocodiles](entry:saltwater-crocodile) could be: in croc country, keep out of the water and stay well back from the edge [ref:crocwise]. The crocodile recorded around Karma Waters is the [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile), *[ngawurr-ngawun](word:ngawurr-ngawun)* [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:ala]. It is usually shy, but a big one can give a serious bite [ref:am-johnstoni].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
**The law.** Freshwater turtles are protected native animals under Queensland's *Nature Conservation Act 1992*, and anyone else needs a licence or permit to take them [ref:qld-nca]. If a turtle takes your bait, unhook it gently and let it go.

**Native title.** The 2013 Western Yalanji determinations recognise rights to **hunt, fish and gather on the land and waters for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal purposes** [ref:brady2013]. A further Western Yalanji determination followed in August 2026 [ref:nit2026wy]. Section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* means native title holders hunting for those needs do not need the licences and permits other people need [ref:alrc].

**At [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters).** The station's agreement with the Western Yalanji Traditional Owners was the first on pastoral land in Australia [ref:karma]. Ask the Traditional Owners before taking anything from their country, and follow the station's rules: no weapons or hunting dogs, and no recreation access from 1 December to 1 April [ref:karma-camping].

**At Karma Waters.** Karma Waters Station falls under the earlier 1998 *Western Yalanji or 'Sunset' Peoples v Pedersen* consent determination, the first consent determination of native title over a pastoral property in Australia [ref:wyac2020] [ref:kw-about]. See the [Karma Waters guide](/dictionaries/kuku_yalanji/country/places/karma-waters) for what it covers, and ask the Traditional Owners and the station before hunting, fishing or gathering.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *[ngujay](word:ngujay)* 'freshwater turtle'; *[ngawiya](word:ngawiya)* '[sea turtle](entry:sea-turtle)'; *[kadan](word:kadan)* 'shell of turtle'; *[diburr](word:diburr)* 'egg'; *[jamal](word:jamal)* 'white of egg'; *[birukay](word:birukay)* 'yolk of the egg'; *[mala-kural](word:mala-kural)* 'good diver'; *[baral](word:baral)* 'to feel something', as in *nyulu nguwul-nguwulbu torch baran-baral* 'He was feeling for his torch in the dark' [ref:hershberger1982].
